text: Vienna in November. Rain, coffee and spies.
That will be London.
Somewhere out there, the Nightglass plans are waiting for a diplomatic bag. They leave at midnight.
An Alpine landscape. Hotel art: pleasant and forgettable. Like me, professionally speaking.
A walnut wardrobe. My evening clothes are hanging inside.
Just my trench coat and a few hangers now.
Dinner jacket, bow tie, cufflinks. The Karvonians will think I'm a banker.
A brass reading lamp. Warm light for a cold job.
The writing desk has a single drawer.
Hotel stationery and a Gideon Bible. Nothing I need.
A handful of schillings. Emergency funds, courtesy of Her Majesty's Treasury.
My briefcase. The locks are keyed to my thumbprint. Very 1987.
Spare shirts, a shaving kit and a paperback. The fun gadget is in my pocket.
Standard issue from Technical Section: one fountain pen.
Twist the cap and it fires a single sleeping dart. One shot, so I'd better make it count.
Turned down, with a chocolate on the pillow. Tempting.
No time. The microfilm leaves Vienna at midnight.
A portable cassette player. The mixtape inside is labelled "Songs to Defect To".
Later. A little synth-pop never cracked a safe.
I already had one. Discipline, Harrow.
Marzipan, nougat and dark chocolate. The best thing about this hotel.
Mozart chocolates on the pillow. Marzipan, nougat and dark chocolate.
I'll leave it. The Karvonians search guests at the door, and a camera that size raises questions.
A subminiature camera, small enough to hide in a cigarette packet. Every spy's best friend.
It's ringing. Nobody calls a hotel room at this hour for good news.
A black rotary telephone. Almost certainly bugged.
Control said radio silence from here on. No more calls.
The door to the hallway.
Not with the phone ringing. It could be London.
Harrow.
Control here. The microfilm is inside the Karvonian Consulate, as we feared.
Colonel Vasko is hosting a reception there tonight. You're going to be his guest.
Without an invitation, I suppose.
Our contact has one for you. She'll be at Café Adler, across the square.
The recognition phrase is: "Does the Danube look blue to you tonight?"
She answers: "Only when it rains."
And if she doesn't?
Then you've asked a stranger about the colour of a river. Good luck, Harrow. This call never happened.
The dome of the Karlskirche. Baroque, beautiful, and bugged by at least three embassies.
In this rain, the whole square looks like an oil painting. A gloomy one.
Posters for Die Fledermaus at the State Opera, and a pop concert at the Stadthalle. Vienna does both with a straight face.
A little yellow car with Munich plates. Someone's West German cousin is visiting.
Stealing a car is loud. Walking is quiet.
Warm light, strong coffee, Viennese gossip. Half the spies in Europe drink here.
My hotel. Five stars, and a doorman who works for the Russians.
Café Adler. The contact should be inside.
Tonight's Abendpost. Colonel Vasko's moustache takes up half the front page.
An old man in a flat cap. He's probably sold papers here since the Habsburgs.
At the end of the avenue: red flags and floodlights. The Karvonian Consulate.
You already have the last copy, sir!
I'll take a paper... ah. My money is back in the hotel room.
Then the news will have to wait for you, mein Herr.
Four schillings. The last evening edition. Danke schön!
I should read this. Right-click it in my inventory.
Evening paper, sir? Hot off the press and wet from the rain.
I'll take a paper.
Anything interesting in the news?
The Karvonians are throwing a party. Their Colonel is on page one again.
Vain as a peacock, that one. They say he has his own face on his cufflinks.
What do you know about the Karvonian Consulate?
Big black cars. Big men with no necks. And tonight, champagne by the crate.
Back home, the Colonel's birthday is practically a national holiday.
Goodbye.
Servus! Mind the puddles.
Slivovitz, Obstler, Williams pear. The Austrian answer to central heating.
Sachertorte. Chocolate, apricot jam, and a century of lawsuits over who owns the recipe.
Franz would notice. Franz notices everything.
Newspapers on wooden holders, the Viennese way. Moscow, Paris and London side by side. Something for every spy in the room.
A brass espresso machine older than I am, and better maintained.
Rain on the glass and the square beyond. Nobody followed me. I think.
My reflection looks tired. Occupational hazard.
A gramophone playing a slightly warped Glenn Miller record.
Better not touch it. The contact might think it's a signal.
A grey homburg and somebody's umbrella. Nobody in Vienna trusts the weather.
The barman. A moustache like a boot brush and eyes that miss nothing.
Platinum hair, red coat, and a cigarette she isn't really smoking. That's my contact, or my funeral.
I don't drink on duty, Mr. Harrow.
Grüß Gott. What can I get you, mein Herr?
A Melange, please.
Bitte sehr. On the house, for a gentleman who says please.
Perfect. Now I can face the Cold War.
Who is the lady in red?
Fräulein Ilse. Every evening she orders one coffee, smokes ten cigarettes and speaks to nobody.
Perhaps you will be the exception.
Heard anything about the Karvonian party?
Their waiters came here for ice this afternoon. Forty bottles of champagne, for eighty guests.
And the old Baron von Katz is invited. Somebody will get very drunk. Probably him.
Nothing, thanks.
Bitte. I am here if you need me.
Why are you still here? Vasko's safe won't open itself.
Remember, Jack: that man is in love with himself. Every detail of his life is about him.
This table is taken.
Lovely evening, isn't it?
It is raining, and you are boring me.
Can I buy you a drink?
I have a coffee. And standards.
Sorry to bother you.
Does the Danube look blue to you tonight?
...Only when it rains.
You are late, Mr. Harrow. Don't sit down. Just listen.
Vasko keeps the microfilm in a wall safe in his private office, upstairs in the consulate.
Here is your invitation. Guests only, black tie. Try not to embarrass me.
And the combination for the safe?
Nobody knows it but Vasko. But he is the vainest man in Vienna. Everything he owns is about himself.
Tonight the whole consulate is celebrating his birthday. Think about that.
And if there are guards on the stairs?
Karvonian soldiers never leave their posts... unless there is a scandal. They hate a scandal.
Neoclassical columns, floodlights, and a lot of men with rifles. Karvonian taste.
A Tatra 613 with diplomatic plates. The chauffeur is pretending to read a newspaper upside down.
A striped sentry box. Empty. Everyone is at the front door tonight.
Warm light, red carpet, and a string quartet playing inside.
Halt! Guests only. Invitation, please.
A Karvonian soldier. He looks like he was carved out of the same stone as the building.
Put him to sleep in front of twenty others? I'd be the next one on the floor.
Are you trying to bribe a soldier of Karvonia? With FOUR schillings?
Please go inside, sir. The Colonel does not like empty rooms.
Good evening.
Halt. This is a private reception. Black tie only.
You look like the detective from a cheap film.
Everyone's a critic. My dinner jacket is back at the hotel.
Good evening, sir. Your invitation, please.
It must be in my other jacket.
Then you and your other jacket may wait outside.
An invitation is not enough, sir. Black tie only. You are dressed for a funeral in the rain.
My dinner jacket is back at the hotel.
Mr. J. Harrow, British Trade Council. Welcome to Karvonia, sir.
Enjoy the celebration of the Colonel's birthday.
Colonel Dragan Vasko, painted as a war hero. The only battle he ever won was against good taste.
A Viennese concert grand, black as a hearse. Nobody has touched it all night.
Chopsticks, in front of eighty diplomats? That would be one way to get noticed.
A champagne tower. One wrong move and it's the most expensive domino rally in Vienna.
I'd bring the whole tower down. The waiter has glasses on his tray.
Diplomats, generals and their wives, waltzing like nothing is wrong. Maybe for them, nothing is.
The staircase is unguarded now. Vasko's office is up there.
The staircase to the private floor. And one very large guard.
Sir! The upper floor is private. Please return to the reception.
A waiter with a silver tray and a smile he gets paid for.
A red-faced aristocrat with a monocle and an empty glass. The glass seems to offend him deeply.
Tempting. But a sleeping baron is a lot less useful than a noisy one.
He's guarding the stairs like his pension depends on it. It probably does.
Lovely party.
The upper floor is private, sir. Please enjoy the reception.
Shoot a soldier in the middle of a crowded ballroom? Subtle, Harrow. Very subtle.
Not on duty, sir.
You still have a full glass, sir. Enjoy.
Champagne, sir?
Yes, thank you.
Dom Pérignon, seventy-eight. Compliments of the Colonel.
Who is the gentleman with the monocle?
Baron von Katz. He has asked me for champagne eleven times. I am instructed to stop at ten.
Between us, sir, he becomes... very loud.
No, thank you.
Ah! Another Englishman! Or Swiss? You all look the same in black.
And you are?
Baron Friedrich von Katz. Eleventh of my name. Last of my fortune.
Enjoying the party?
I would be, if these barbarians refilled my glass! A Baron, left DRY! It is a scandal!
A scandal. How interesting.
What do you think of Colonel Vasko?
Dreadful bore. He makes us toast his portrait every hour. "Happy birthday, dear Dragan..."
Forty-one years old and still no taste in wine.
Excuse me.
Go, go. And send me a waiter!
Baron. Allow me.
At last! A man of culture!
LADIES AND GENTLEMEN! A TOAST!
TO COLONEL VASKO... AND HIS MAGNIFICENT, RIDICULOUS MOUSTACHE!
Happy birthday to yoooou... in a dictatorship toooo...
Sir! You are making a scene!
A scene? My dear boy, I AM the scene!
Please come with me, sir. Some fresh air.
Karvonians hate a scandal. Ilse was right.
Vasko's office. Portrait, flag, safe. The man decorated a room around his own face.
An even bigger portrait of Vasko. Two in one building. That tells you everything about the man.
"COL. D. VASKO." In case he forgets his own face.
The Collected Speeches of Colonel Vasko, volumes one to nine. The spines have never been cracked.
The flag of the People's Republic of Karvonia. Red, for reasons nobody will say out loud.
A desk the size of a small country. Karvonia, for example.
Invoices, a signed photograph of himself... and a birthday card.
"To my little Dragan, forty-one today! Love, Mama." A desk calendar has today circled in red: the 14th of November, 1987.
A typewriter with a fresh ribbon. The last letter is still on the roller.
"Shipment confirmed. Friday. Karvograd, platform nine." Interesting.
A reel-to-reel recorder, wired into the telephone line. Vasko bugs his own calls.
Tempting, but there's no time to listen to eight hours of Vasko.
A globe that opens into a drinks cabinet. Karvonia is painted twice its real size.
Plum brandy and a bottle of French cognac. No microfilm. Worth a look, though.
A banker's lamp. The only green thing in Karvonia.
A wall safe with a six-digit electronic keypad. West German, very expensive.
Empty now, apart from a spare jar of moustache wax.
Snoring like a tractor. He'll wake up with a headache and no idea what happened.
A Karvonian guard with a pistol pointed at my chest.
Sweet dreams, soldier.
Easy, soldier. I'm just here to fix the plumbing.
In a dinner jacket? Hands UP!
He's had enough for one night.
I do not drink with thieves!
Not with a pistol in my back.
Back down the stairs? Every guard in the building is on his way up.
A window onto the rooftops. Searchlights are sweeping the sky out there.
Not until I have what I came for.
He'd shoot me before I got the latch open.
The rooftops it is. Ilse said she'd have a car waiting on the Ring.
A steel canister, stamped NIGHTGLASS. Got you.
STOP! Hands where I can see them!
You again! HANDS UP!
What th...
Ten seconds to lights-out, just as Technical Section promised.
Too slow, English. GUARDS! UP HERE!
Born on the 14th of November, 1946. Everything about him is about him. Worth remembering.
Six digits. Ilse said everything Vasko owns is about himself... Day, month, year?
Six digits. I need to know more about the Colonel. Something personal. His desk, or the evening paper, might help.
That phone won't answer itself.
I should check my briefcase before I go anywhere.
The contact is at Café Adler, across the square. A woman who likes rain, apparently.
Black tie tonight, and my dinner jacket is still in the hotel wardrobe.
Dinner jacket, invitation. Time to charm the man at the consulate gate.
That Baron is desperate for a drink, and the waiter has a full tray.
A scandal would pull that guard off the stairs. A thirsty Baron with a full glass, perhaps.
The stairs are clear. Vasko's office is waiting upstairs.
Six digits, and all about Vasko. His desk might tell me something personal.
He's vain enough to use his own birthday. Day, month, year: fourteen, eleven, forty-six.
Out through the window. Over the rooftops to the car.
Dawn. Birdsong. Somewhere a baker is opening up. I'm alive.
Coffee is on the table. Now, let's see what we nearly died for.
Sunrise over the cathedral. Vienna looks innocent at this hour.
An old valve radio, tuned to the morning news.
The news says there was a gas leak at the Karvonian Consulate. No injuries. One very embarrassed Baron.
Strong, black and Viennese. Just what I needed.
A pot of coffee and two cups. She was expecting me to make it back.
Poetry in four languages and a train timetable for the whole Eastern Bloc.
A microfilm viewer that doubles as a projector. It throws the image onto the wall.
I need to put the microfilm in first.
Ilse, looking out at the sunrise. She hasn't said a word about the car chase.
You drive like a getaway pilot.
And you talk like a man who hasn't checked his microfilm yet.
Wing sections. Radar-absorbent panels. The whole aircraft.
Engine intakes, cockpit, weapons bay... Wait. There's one more frame.
A note. "Too slow, Mr. Harrow. The real plans left for Karvonia yesterday."
A decoy. Vasko let me steal it. The real Nightglass is already behind the Iron Curtain.
I know.
Ilse?
I'm sorry, Jack. Vasko pays better than London, and he never sends his people out in the rain.
You set me up.
Someone had to steal the decoy. Now London believes the plans are safe, and nobody goes looking for the real ones.
And me?
You were never here, Mr. Harrow. Remember?
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
A few Austrian schillings. Enough for a newspaper, not enough for a bribe.
Technical Section's finest. Twist the cap and it fires one sleeping dart. Effective range: about four metres.
Wiener Abendpost, evening edition. Colonel Vasko is on the front page, naturally.
"The Consul of the People's Republic of Karvonia requests the pleasure of Mr J. Harrow, British Trade Council." Gold-edged. Very official.
Dom Pérignon, 1978. The workers of Karvonia are very generous tonight.
A steel canister stamped NIGHTGLASS · STRENG GEHEIM. This is what I came for.
Three days ago, the plans for NIGHTGLASS, the West's first invisible stealth fighter, vanished from a hangar in the Nevada desert.
It ends here, at the consulate of the People's Republic of Karvonia. Tonight its military attaché, Colonel Dragan Vasko, is throwing himself a birthday gala.
At midnight the microfilm leaves Vienna in a diplomatic bag. Nobody can touch a diplomatic bag. So it must never reach one.
Your name is Jack Harrow. Officially, you are not in Austria.
The car is waiting at the bottom of the cable, engine running. Ilse drives without a word.
Dawn over Vienna. Ilse's attic smells of coffee and gun oil. The microfilm is still warm in Jack's pocket.
Who pulled the trigger?
